blocks.title: Functions
blocks.subtitle: One input, exactly one output
blocks.narration: Chapter three. Functions are the machines of mathematics: one input, exactly one output. We define them precisely, find their natural domains, test their symmetry, chain them by composition, and reverse them with inverses. Then the two transcendental families — exponentials and logarithms — power every growth and decay model in the course.

blocks.heading: What Is a Function?
bullets: each input gives exactly one output
vertical line test on the graph
blocks.formula_caption: f maps the domain D into the reals
blocks.narration: A function is a rule assigning to every input x in the domain D exactly one output, f of x. Exactly one — that is the entire contract. The domain collects the allowed inputs; the range collects the outputs actually produced. On a graph, the vertical line test enforces the contract: any vertical line may cross the picture at most once. A full circle fails — almost every x there corresponds to two y values. The notation reads: f maps D into the reals, and x maps to f of x.

blocks.heading: The Natural Domain
blocks.narration: The natural domain is the largest set of real inputs for which the formula makes sense. Only three obstructions ever occur. Division demands a nonzero denominator. An even root, such as a square root, demands a nonnegative radicand. A logarithm demands a strictly positive argument. For a complicated formula, write down the condition from each ingredient and intersect them all. These three rules settle every domain question in weeks one to four — and most domain questions on the test.

blocks.heading: Even and Odd Symmetry
blocks.formula_caption: even on the left, odd on the right
blocks.narration: Symmetry comes in two flavors. A function is even when f of minus x equals f of x — the graph mirrors across the y axis, like the absolute value of x plus one. It is odd when f of minus x equals minus f of x — the graph survives a half-turn about the origin. The plot shows p of x equals x cubed minus four x. Only odd powers appear, so p is odd: change the sign of x, and the output flips sign. The curve crosses the axis at minus two, zero, and two — the marked point. Mixed powers, like x cubed plus x squared, have neither symmetry.

blocks.heading: Composition and Inverses
bullets: inverse: solve y = f(x) for x
graphs mirror in the line y = x
blocks.narration: Composition chains two machines: feed x to g, then feed the result to f. That is f after g, written f of g of x. Order genuinely matters — the next example shows f after g and g after f giving different functions. The inverse runs the machine backwards: solve y equals f of x for x. Only one-to-one functions have inverses — checked by the horizontal line test — and the graph of the inverse mirrors the original across the line y equals x. Compose a function with its inverse, and you recover plain x.

blocks.heading: Exponentials and Logarithms
bullets: log of product = sum of logs
ln and exp undo each other
blocks.formula: \log_b x = y \iff b^y = x, \quad \log_b(xy) = \log_b x + \log_b y
blocks.narration: Exponential and logarithm are two views of one fact. The logarithm base b of x is the exponent y such that b to the y equals x — that is the definition on screen. The laws follow: the log of a product is the sum of the logs; the log of a quotient is a difference; a power slides out front as a factor. The natural pair, e to the x and ln of x, undo each other. Every growth or decay model has the form A of t equals A zero times e to the k t: positive k grows, negative k decays, and the doubling time is ln two over k.

blocks.heading: Finding Domains
blocks.narration: Two domain hunts. First, the square root of five minus two x. The root demands a nonnegative radicand: five minus two x at least zero, so x is at most five halves. The domain is everything up to five halves, with the bracket closed at five halves. Second, the square root of x plus two over x minus one. We need the quotient nonnegative and x different from one. The critical points are minus two and one. Testing the intervals: the quotient is nonnegative up to minus two, and again strictly beyond one. The domain is everything up to minus two, closed, union the open ray from one onward.

blocks.heading: f∘g versus g∘f
blocks.narration: Let f of x be two x minus three, and g of x be x squared plus one. First, f after g: substitute g into f — two times x squared plus one, minus three — which simplifies to two x squared minus one. Now the other order, g after f: square the whole of two x minus three, then add one — four x squared minus twelve x plus ten. Different functions: check x equals zero, where the first gives minus one and the second gives ten. Composition is not commutative — shift then square is not square then shift. Self-composition, like g after g, is perfectly legal too.

blocks.heading: Battery Discharge
blocks.narration: A battery discharges: E of t equals E zero times e to the minus zero point zero two five t, with t in hours. What fraction survives ten hours? Divide by E zero: e to the minus zero point two five is about zero point seven seven eight — roughly seventy eight percent remains. When is half left? Set the exponential to one half: t equals the natural log of two over zero point zero two five — about twenty seven point seven hours. And why is zero never reached? The exponential is strictly positive at every finite time; it approaches zero only as t tends to infinity — our first honest limit.

blocks.heading: Classes of Functions
blocks.narration: A vocabulary table. Linear: three x minus seven — a straight line. Polynomial: x to the fourth minus two x plus one — smooth everywhere. Rational: a ratio of polynomials, like x plus one over x squared plus four — defined wherever the denominator is nonzero. Algebraic: roots of polynomials, like the square root of x squared plus one. Exponential: two to the x — the variable lives in the exponent, so it is transcendental. Trigonometric: sine x — also transcendental. The classes overlap: every polynomial is also algebraic, so always name the smallest class.

items: f∘g ≠ g∘f; inverse mirrors in y = x
blocks.narration: Chapter three compressed. A function assigns each input exactly one output, and the vertical line test checks it. Domains are blocked only by division, even roots, and logarithms. Even functions mirror across the axis; odd ones rotate about the origin. Composition order matters, and inverses undo one-to-one functions. The logarithm is simply the exponent. Now, the main event: limits.

blocks.title: Limits: The Core Idea
blocks.subtitle: What does approaching really mean?
blocks.narration: Chapter four — the heart of the course. Limits answer two questions at once: how fast is something changing right now, and what value is a function heading toward? We build the idea from secant slopes and average speeds, sharpen it into one-sided and infinite limits, make it precise with epsilon and delta, and apply it to real engineering systems.

blocks.heading: Two Founding Problems
bullets: shrink the step h toward zero
blocks.formula_caption: the instantaneous rate is defined as a limit
blocks.narration: Calculus is born from two questions. How steeply does a curve rise at a single point? How fast does an object move at a single instant? Both answers use the same trick. The slope of the secant line through two nearby points is the change in f over the change in x. The average velocity over a time interval is displacement over time. Now shrink the interval. The average rates approach a number, and that number is defined as the limit on screen: f of a plus h minus f of a, over h, as h tends to zero. This limit is the derivative — the instantaneous rate.

blocks.heading: Robot Cart: Average to Instantaneous
blocks.narration: A robot cart moves with position s of t equals two t squared plus three t, in meters. What is its speed at t equals two? Anchor first: s of two is eight plus six — fourteen meters. Expand s of two plus h: fourteen plus eleven h plus two h squared. The average speed over the interval is the difference, eleven h plus two h squared, divided by h. Cancel h: eleven plus two h. Now let h tend to zero — the leftover two h dies, and the averages close in on eleven from both sides. The instantaneous speed at t equals two is exactly eleven meters per second.

blocks.heading: The Limit of a Function
bullets: x approaches a, never equals a
f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L
the value f(a) itself is ignored
a limit, when it exists, is unique
blocks.formula_caption: the limit of f of x, as x approaches a, equals L
blocks.narration: The central definition. We say the limit of f of x, as x approaches a, equals L, when the values f of x get arbitrarily close to L as x gets close to a — from both sides, but never actually reaching a. Three remarks. The point itself is ignored: f may be undefined at a, or defined to be anything else. When a limit exists, it is unique — no function approaches two numbers at once. And this is a guarantee: for every closeness demanded of f, some closeness of x must deliver it.

blocks.heading: One-Sided Limits
bullets: left limit: x → a from below
right limit: x → a from above
blocks.formula: \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L
blocks.formula_caption: the limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits agree
blocks.narration: Approaching from the left and from the right gives two one-sided limits. The criterion on screen is the workhorse of the course: the two-sided limit exists exactly when the left and the right limits exist and are equal. At every piecewise junction, compute both branches. Quick example: a function equal to two x plus one below x equals two, and seven minus x above it. Left limit: five. Right limit: five. Equal — so the limit is five, and the pieces join seamlessly. When they disagree, the two-sided limit simply does not exist — as the next example shows.

blocks.heading: Switching System: a Voltage Step
blocks.narration: A switching device outputs two t plus one volts below t equals four, and twelve minus t volts from four onward. At t equals four: from the left, the first branch gives two times four plus one — nine volts. From the right, the second branch gives twelve minus four — eight volts. Nine versus eight: the one-sided limits disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist. Physically, the output steps down by one volt the instant the threshold is crossed. Sharp steps can excite transients in the controlled device — which is why engineers often soften switching with filters or soft-start logic.

blocks.heading: Why 1/x Blows Up at Zero
blocks.narration: Watch the two curves. The yellow one is one over x. Just right of zero it climbs without end — however small x is, the output is enormous. Just left of zero it plunges without end: the left limit is minus infinity, the right limit plus infinity. The blue curve, minus one over x, is its mirror through the origin. Both hug the dashed vertical line x equals zero without ever touching it — the vertical asymptote. And notice how both flatten toward zero as x runs far left or far right — a first glimpse of a horizontal asymptote.

blocks.heading: The Precise Definition: Epsilon and Delta

parts.note: the tolerance — how close f(x) must be to L
the radius — how close x must be to a
x within delta of a, but not equal

blocks.narration: Now the precise engine beneath the intuition — read it with me. The limit of f of x as x approaches a equals L if and only if: for every epsilon greater than zero — the yellow tolerance, how close f of x must stay to L — there exists a delta greater than zero — the blue radius — such that whenever x is within delta of a but not equal to a — the green condition — then f of x is within epsilon of L — the red guarantee. In pictures: x lives in a delta band around a, and f of x must answer in an epsilon band around L. Any challenge epsilon must be met with a working delta.

blocks.heading: The First Standard Limit
bullets: the angle must be in radians
blocks.formula_caption: sine of x over x tends to one at zero
blocks.narration: The most famous limit of the course: sine of x, divided by x. At zero this is zero over zero — undefined. But near zero the ratio tends to one, provided x measures radians — that caveat is essential. The numbers tell the story: at x equal to one tenth, the ratio is zero point nine nine eight three; at one hundredth, zero point nine nine nine nine eight; at one thousandth, seven nines then an eight. The proof squeezes the ratio between cosine and one; both bounds approach one, forcing the ratio to one. Keep this limit in your pocket — chapter six leans on it constantly.

blocks.heading: RC Circuit: Charging to a Limit
blocks.result: 0 V at the start; 12 V in the limit
blocks.narration: An RC circuit charges toward a twelve-volt supply: V of t equals twelve times one minus e to the minus t over R C, with the time constant R times C equal to one second. At the very start the exponential is e to the zero — one — so V starts at zero: an uncharged capacitor. As time grows, e to the minus t decays to zero, so V tends to twelve times one minus zero — twelve volts, the supply level. The approach is asymptotic: roughly sixty three percent charged after one time constant, ninety nine percent after five. Engineers say it in limit language: V tends to the supply as t tends to infinity.

Chapter four, distilled. Average rates become instantaneous rates through a limit. The two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits agree. One over x blows up at zero — a vertical asymptote. Epsilon and delta make arbitrarily close precise and checkable. And sine of x over x tends to one — in radians. Next: computing limits systematically.
